content.text:
Humanity has always been fascinated by the shapes of the things around them. In some early cave paintings, the sun is depicted as a circle. In the cave paintings of Gudahandi in Odisha, one sees numerous geometric patterns including triangles, squares, circles, and ovals. These shapes were likely inspired by what humans saw in nature. Can you recognise the origin of these shapes?
Circles form when raindrops fall on water. The cross-section of a plant stem and the inflorescence of a sunflower are also circular in shape. The full moon and sun also look circular.
What properties are common to all circles, big and small? You have studied one such property in Grade 7. Humans must have noticed it after observing many circular patterns in nature. Every circle has a centre. All points on the circle are at equal distance from the centre. We turn this observation around and make it the definition of a circle.
Activity: List some objects from nature that resemble a circle.

content.text:
When we talk of mathematical shapes such as circles, triangles and squares, we always assume that the figures are drawn on a piece of paper, a two-dimensional plane.
A circle is the set of all points on the plane that are equidistant from a given point on that plane. The set of points that satisfy a given condition is also called the locus of points that satisfy the condition. Using this term, a circle can also be described as the locus of points that are equidistant from a given point. The given point is the centre of the circle. The distance from the centre to any point on the circle is the radius of the circle.
In the figure, A is the centre of the circle. All points on the plane at a distance equal to the length of AB from A form a circle with centre A and radius equal to the length of AB.
Let B and C be two points on the circle. The line segment BC is called a chord of the circle. The angle subtended by the chord BC at the centre is angle BAC. A chord passing through the centre of a circle is called a diameter.

content.text:
What makes circles so appealing is that they are perfectly symmetrical. Say you are looking at a wheel of a vehicle. You see a point of the wheel touching the ground. When you look at the wheel again after some time, you again see a point of the wheel touching the ground. Can you tell if the two points are the same point? There is no way you can tell; a rotating wheel looks the same at all times! We say the circle has complete rotational symmetry: rotate it by any angle and it looks exactly the same.
Draw a circle on the paper and cut along the circle. Fold the circular paper so that the boundaries overlap, then open it. You see a crease; it is a line of reflection symmetry of the circle. Does this line pass through the centre of the circle? It does. It is a diameter of the circle. All diameters are lines of reflection symmetry.

content.text:
Now that we have defined a circle and listed some of its properties, let us ask this question: Given two points A and B on a plane, how many circles pass through A and B?
If a circle passes through A and B, it has a centre, say O. The lengths OA and OB are equal. Is there another point with this property? Yes, the midpoint of segment AB. With the midpoint as centre, a circle passing through A and B can be drawn. Its radius is half the length of AB, and AB is a diameter.
Are there more circles passing through both A and B? Clearly, any point equidistant from A and B can be the centre of a circle passing through A and B. Do you know of such points? We have seen that the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from A and B, and every point that is equidistant from A and B is on the perpendicular bisector! So, the centres of all circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
In the figure, we see circles through points A and B, and through C and D, and the perpendicular bisector of CD. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the centre of a circle passing through C and D. So we have circles with centres K, J and L containing points C and D.

It is natural to ask: How many circles can you draw through three distinct points A, B and C on a plane? Is there always at least one such circle? Not necessarily! What if A, B and C lie on a straight line, i.e., are collinear? Can you explain why, in this case, there is no circle through A, B and C?
Let us assume that A, B and C are not collinear. Is there always a circle passing through A, B and C? Can there be more than one circle through A, B and C?

content.text:
Why is this true? If there is a circle that passes through non-collinear A, B and C, the circle must have a centre. Let's call that centre O (we will discover O soon).
Since OA = OB, we know that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Since OA = OC, we know that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC as well.
But A, B and C are not collinear. So, the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC will intersect at a unique point, since two intersecting lines meet at exactly one point on the plane. That point must be O.
Using O as the centre we can draw a circle with radius equal to the length of OA. That will pass through A, B and C. This explains why the statement is true.
Now three non-collinear points also determine a triangle. What we have described above is the construction of a circle that passes through the vertices of the triangle.
The centre O of the circle that passes through the vertices A, B and C of ΔABC is called the circumcentre of ΔABC. The circle is called the circumcircle and is said to circumscribe the triangle. Conversely, the triangle is said to be inscribed in the circle. Since, the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC is a single point, there is just one such circle for a given triangle. Further, for an acute-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies inside the triangle. For an obtuse-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies outside the triangle. And for a right-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

content.text:
Theorem 1: There is a unique circle passing through three non-collinear points.
Given: A, B and C are three points that are not collinear.
To show: Exactly one circle passes through A, B and C.
1. Suppose a circle passes through A, B and C; call its centre O.
2. OA = OB, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
3. OA = OC, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC.
4. A, B and C are not collinear, so these two bisectors are not parallel.
5. Two intersecting lines meet at exactly one point, so O is that one point.
6. With centre O and radius OA, the circle passes through A, B and C.
7. There is only one choice of O, so the circle is unique.

Draw and Decide, Q1: A, B and C are three collinear points. Can you find a point P such that PA = PB = PC? What can you say about the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC? Draw and check. Can you show that for three collinear points A, B and C, the perpendicular bisector of AB and BC are parallel? Is it possible for a circle to pass through collinear points? media.tool_name: Spin the wheel: what does the centre see?
media.description: Spin the wheel: what does the centre see?. You drag a chord all the way round a circle: dragging its body or either endpoint rotates it, its length stays fixed, and the angle it makes at the centre C refuses to change. A length stepper changes the chord's length instead, and each distinct value logs a row in a table. You can add a second chord with its own stepper, and when the two lengths match, their angles at C match too. Once you ask for it, the two radii to each chord's ends are drawn; once you ask again, you can lock the angle at C and try, and fail, to change the chord's length. Starting scene: One circle, centre C marked, one chord at a seeded angle with length equal to the radius. No radii are drawn. The readout strip shows the chord's length and its angle at C. Open question: A thread is tied across a wheel. Spin the wheel. What does the centre see? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Take the thread all the way round the wheel. What changed? (2) Now make the thread longer. What moved with it? (3) Join both ends of the thread to the centre. What shape do you see? (4) Two of the three sides are always the radius. So what decides the triangle's shape? (5) Lock the angle at the centre. Now try to change the chord. Break it: Lock the angle at the centre (rung 5): the chord still rotates freely, but the length stepper springs back every time you try to change it, refusing the resize. That refusal is the discovery, matching chords cannot match angles and then let one length slip away. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; a chord's length only changes through its stepper, never by dragging. The tutor: The tutor may ask what stayed the same as you spun the wheel and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never says 'subtend', 'congruent', 'SSS', 'SAS' or 'isosceles', never states the result, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your table of lengths and angles, and whether you matched two chords and felt the lock, go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

media.description: Slide the point. Can you light just one lamp?. You slide a point M along a chord AB and watch two lamps: one for 'equal halves' (AM = MB) and one for 'right angle' (the segment from the centre meets the chord at 90 degrees). The two lamps light together only at one spot, the foot, and never separately, however hard you try. You can also drag the chord's ends to try a new chord, and, once you ask for it, move the line's starting point off the centre to see the two lamps come apart. Starting scene: A circle, centre C, one chord AB at a seeded position, and a point M on the chord deliberately off the midpoint. The segment CM is drawn. Both lamps are off. Open question: Slide the point along the thread. Can you light just one lamp? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Slide the point along the chord. Watch the two halves. (2) Now watch the angle at the same time. (3) Try to light just one lamp. (4) Join the centre to both ends of the chord. Two triangles, what is the same in each? (5) The two angles at the point are equal, and they sit on a straight line. So how big is each? Break it: Move the line's start off the centre (rung 3): the length lamp still lights at the midpoint, but the angle lamp now lights somewhere else entirely, and the two lamps come apart. That is why the theorem says 'from the centre'. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; M always stays on the chord, between A and B. The tutor: The tutor may ask which lamp lit first (neither, that's the point) and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never says 'perpendicular bisector', 'congruent', 'bisects' or 'linear pair', never says the two conditions are equivalent, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; how many chords you tried, how many times you failed to light just one lamp, and whether you moved the line off the centre, go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

content.text:
You may want to know when 4 points lie on the same circle. That will have to wait till the end of this chapter. We need to do some more work to get there.
Tie a thread at two points on a wheel; pull it tight. The thread can be thought of as a chord of the wheel (a circle). Imagine joining the end points of the thread to the centre. The thread subtends an angle at the centre. Now, rotate the wheel. The thread rotates around the centre along with the wheel.
In the new position, the thread is another chord on the circle. What is common to the first and second chords? They have the same length, equal to the length of the thread. What about the angle subtended by the second chord at the centre? It must surely be the same as the angle subtended by the first chord at the centre. We now explain why this is true.
